coverage.assessment: Two causal links are thinned by the revision: Rome's slave/fetish logic and the post-1500 resistance. The definitions, the spider image and the Rome scandal still connect.
Referents mostly hold. 'Outside of it' and 'this completeness' resolve, and 'this method' (revision p23) resolves loosely to the Baconian law. These points are noted under F3.
There is no dialogue. The Augustine quotation, St. Louis's prayer and the Bacon maxims all remain correctly attributed.
The dates 313, 410 and c.430 are correct, and 'rather recklessly' survives. The self-deprecating historian hedge and the 'so little is known about the mind' disclaimer are cut (F6).
The ending points to a formula of acceleration without stating it. Adams's breakdown at Ara Coeli remains retrospective, and nothing is disclosed early.
Periodic sentences and the mock-commercial Constantine survive. Some passivity imagery (vegetable and forest, 'little or no effort') and the ironic Church concession are lost (F5, F7).
The Civitas Dei thread and the closing convergence argument are weakened (F2, F4). The Virgin/Unity-versus-multiplicity frame otherwise holds.
All three dependencies are intact at both endpoints in the revised drafts of 008, 007 and 027.

The other explains that rapid political growth forced Rome to extend both slave-system and fetish-system. 'Fetish-power was cheap' now lacks its comparison, and the vicious circle no longer ties back to 'too much energy, and too fast.'
findings.counterevidence: The slave-system sentence and 'vicious circle' survive, so the outline remains readable.

strengths: All eight protected excerpts (V1–V8) survive exactly, including the year-300/1900 Isis analogy that closes the historical sweep.
The Edict of Milan is kept 'Regarded as an Act of Congress' together with the stock-broker conceit, preserving the mock-commercial voice.
The Augustine quotation is clearly Augustine's, and the dates 313, the Milvian Bridge 'the year before', 410 and 'towards 430' are accurate.
The final paragraph ends on the need for 'some mechanical formula of acceleration' without stating it, setting up chapter 036.
The 'rather recklessly' hedge, the compass 'educated' line, and St. Louis kneeling before Greek fire are all retained.
summary: The revision is close to the 2,700-word target. It keeps all eight protected excerpts, the planned dates, the Augustine attribution, and the forward-pointing close. It also preserves all three cross-chapter dependencies. Its own new cuts, however, remove several causal links that the first draft had kept: why rapid growth forced Rome to expand slavery and fetish (Rome's two engines); the Civitas Dei as the new attraction whose triumph the new forces interrupt; the established resistance and helplessness before post-1500 forces; and the explicit convergence of Church, philosophy and science in the closing argument. Earlier sections also lose some passivity imagery and hedges. Nothing is misleading enough to require repair, but the losses warrant editorial review. The Rome section runs above its planned weight and the Bacon section below it, so small transfers are feasible.
